question: Which typography and empty-state practices would most improve our static pages?
finding: Our body size and line spacing are fine, but line length and empty states need work.
facts: Practical Typography recommends 15-25px body text, 120-145% line spacing, and 45-90 characters per line.
NN/g says empty states should communicate status, teach what will appear, and link to the next step.
inferences: Our 16px/1.55 body is within range, so the gain is in line length and rhythm.
Our empty Ideas and Research sections fail all three NN/g goals.
existing_work: Design backlog d1-d6 (filters, digest, badges, contrast check)
opportunity: Fix empty states and line length in this sprint
alternatives: Wait for content to fill the sections
success_metric: Empty sections explain themselves; line length at most about 75ch

question: Which interface patterns and capabilities are emerging in leading AI products?
finding: Leading AI products are converging on 'governor' patterns that show the work: an action plan before acting, inline citations, branches, and a gallery of real examples. Slopworks already has the raw material for all four.
facts: The Shape of AI pattern library groups 'Governors' (human-in-the-loop) patterns: Action plan, Branches, Citations.
It lists 'Example gallery' (share sample generations and prompts) and 'Prompt details' (show what is actually happening behind the scenes) as wayfinders.
inferences: Our ideas.json (plan), research.json (citations) and chat threads (branches) map onto these patterns without new data.
An example gallery of worked challenges answers 'what can this team do' faster than a role list.
existing_work: Team chat threads, research notes with sources, decision record i9-i20
opportunity: Lead the showcase with an example gallery of worked challenges, each showing plan, citations, and outcome
alternatives: Keep the role-list home page and add marketing copy
risks: Gallery could look staged if examples are not real traces
experiment: Mock one gallery card from the d4 contrast-check history and see if it answers 'what did they do' in one screen
success_metric: Each gallery card links a real plan, at least one source, and a shipped PR

question: Which no-JS interaction patterns would make Slopworks feel distinctive, intuitive, and polished?
finding: Three platform features give app-like polish with zero scripts: exclusive accordions via details name=, :target step views (already used for filters), and cross-document view transitions opted into with one CSS at-rule. All degrade to plain pages.
facts: MDN: details elements sharing a name attribute form a group where only one is open, giving accordions without scripting.
Chrome docs: cross-document view transitions are opt-in with one CSS at-rule (view-transition, navigation: auto) on same-origin pages; supported in Chrome 126+ and Safari 18.2, not Firefox.
NN/g: motion should be brief and used for feedback, state change, and spatial navigation, not to entertain.
inferences: A Research Arena can show one role's report at a time with details name=, no JS.
View transitions are a safe progressive enhancement: Firefox users get a normal page load.
existing_work: CSS :target/:has() filter chips (#33), focus rings and reduced motion (#32)
opportunity: One interaction kit for the showcase: exclusive accordions, :target steps, page-to-page transitions, all reduced-motion aware
alternatives: Add JS for tabs and animations (blocked by check.py, and that ban stays)
risks: details name= is newer than details itself; older browsers open several at once, which is harmless
experiment: Prototype an exclusive accordion and the view-transition at-rule on two pages; check Firefox fallback and reduced motion
success_metric: No scripts; every pattern works by keyboard and degrades to a readable page

question: What would prospective clients need to understand before trusting an AI automation team?
finding: Hypothesis: clients calibrate trust on ability, reliability, and benevolence, and want limits and data sources stated up front. Our strongest trust asset is visible error-catching, not polish.
facts: Google PAIR: trust factors are ability, reliability, and benevolence; communicate capabilities and limitations early; articulate data sources.
PAIR: indicating a prediction could be wrong may lower trust in that output but raise long-term reliance.
inferences: Our runs already show Verify dropping 10 of 30 backfill candidates and Shield dropping 1 for personal data; that is reliability evidence clients rarely see.
A 'what we can and can't do' block would answer the client's first question honestly.
existing_work: Schedule page limits section; Behind the scenes run counts
opportunity: Landing block: can / can't / how we catch our own mistakes, each linking a real trace
alternatives: Testimonials (we have none, and inventing them is out)
risks: Demand claim is untested; no client or reader feedback exists
experiment: Ryno reads a draft landing and answers the three CEO questions in under 30 seconds
success_metric: CEO proxy test answers all three questions from the landing alone

question: What interactive experience could set Slopworks apart from conventional agent dashboards?
finding: A 'follow one decision' explorer: pick a shipped change and step through pitch, research, challenge, score, PR sign-offs, and Trial's check, every step a real link. Dashboards show status; this shows reasoning.
facts: Explorable Explanations describes itself as a hub for learning through play, built by people reuniting play and learning.
PAIR lists 'explanation via interaction' (let users ask 'what if?') as a way to build mental models and trust.
inferences: Most agent dashboards show live status; few let a visitor replay why a decision was made.
:target steps make a stepper possible with no JS.
existing_work: ideas.json decision record links research, scores, and Trial checks; PR comments hold sign-offs
opportunity: Case files: 2 real decisions (d4 contrast check, d1 filters vs the input ban) as step-through stories
risks: Thin cases feel padded; only use decisions with real friction
experiment: Write one case file as plain Markdown first and count how many steps have a real link
success_metric: Every step in a case file links a commit, PR comment, chat message, or research note

question: Which proposed experiences look impressive but add little practical value?
finding: Cut: a pulsing 'live' activity view (we run once a day), simulated agent playback, numeric confidence percentages, and an Impact Ledger with no measurements. Challenge: demo challenges invented by the team prove less than replaying real work.
facts: NN/g: motion attracts attention whether meaningful or not; gratuitous animation distracts, and attention hijacking is a dark pattern.
PAIR: numeric confidence presumes users understand probability and can be misleading; categorical buckets are an alternative.
inferences: A 'live' feed on a once-a-day routine would be misleading on 23 hours of every day.
Real case files (contrast catch, input-ban workaround) beat invented demos as proof; demos should come second.
existing_work: Avatar idle animation already respects reduced motion (#17, #32)
opportunity: Ship real case files before the first demo challenge; drop live-activity and ledger ideas until data exists
alternatives: Build all five experiences at once (rejected by CEO brief too)
risks: Cutting too much could leave the landing flat; keep one strong visual
experiment: Score each cut against 'what can it prove it accomplished?'; anything with no real artifact stays cut
success_metric: Nothing on the showcase claims liveness, metrics, or outcomes without a linked artifact

question: Which concepts fit the static architecture, and which would need new infrastructure?
finding: Living Team, Research Arena, case files, and demo challenges all fit: build.py renders them from JSON. Live activity, visitor challenges, and analytics need servers or input and stay out. Pages terms on commercial sites need Ryno's read.
facts: GitHub Pages limits: published sites up to 1 GB, soft 100 GB/month bandwidth, soft 10 builds/hour.
GitHub Pages is not intended to run an online business or a site primarily directed at commercial transactions or SaaS.
inferences: A showcase that describes the team's work is not a transaction site, but pitching for clients moves closer to that line.
One new data file (cases/challenges) plus schema is the only data-model change needed.
existing_work: build.py renders 15 static files from data/*.json; schemas in data/schema
opportunity: Add data/cases.json (real case files and labeled demos) with a schema linking research ids, chat ids, and PR numbers
alternatives: A JS framework or backend (breaks free-tier and no-script rules)
risks: Commercial framing vs Pages terms; page weight as pages grow
experiment: Draft the cases schema and validate one case file in CI
success_metric: Every new page builds from repo data with build --check green and under the page-weight budget

question: Which experience could ship first as a compelling working prototype?
finding: The Research Arena: this research round already exists as structured data (14 reports, facts vs inferences, Critic's challenge, Coordinator's scores), so a page can render it next PR with no new data model.
facts: MDN: details/summary is baseline widely available since January 2020 and needs no script.
data/research.json already separates facts, inferences, evidence, confidence, and status per report.
inferences: The Arena is the only concept where the content is done and only rendering remains.
Shipping it first gives later pages (case files, challenges) a reusable card and label system.
existing_work: Team chat Research section renders the latest note per role
opportunity: An /arena/ page for this round: question, each role's answer, the challenge, the scores, the decision
alternatives: Start with the landing (needs proof content to link to first)
risks: Page weight with 14 reports; keep reports collapsed by default
experiment: Render the Arena from today's data locally and check weight and keyboard use
success_metric: Arena page builds from research.json and ideas.json only, under the weight budget

question: How can the interface make verified findings, hypotheses, and recommendations obviously different?
finding: Use a fixed, small vocabulary like intelligence analysts do: separate certain knowledge from reasoned judgment, use a few standard likelihood words, and pair them with a confidence level. Our data already has the fields.
facts: Sherman Kent's goal (1964) was to make clear what is certain knowledge and what is reasoned judgment, and what degree of certitude lies behind each.
The US National Intelligence Council pairs a small set of likelihood words with confidence levels (high, moderate, low).
inferences: Three visual tiers fit our data: Verified fact (facts + source), Hypothesis (inferences), Recommendation (decision with scores).
Words, not percentages: we have no calibrated probabilities.
existing_work: research.json status and confidence fields; facts and inferences split (#20)
opportunity: A shared label kit: Verified / Hypothesis / Recommendation / Demo, each with icon, text, and color, never color alone
risks: Too many badges become noise; cap at one tier label plus confidence per claim
experiment: Relabel 3 existing research cards and check each claim lands in exactly one tier
success_metric: Every claim on a showcase page carries exactly one tier label

question: With no visitor input, what data on the showcase still needs protection?
finding: The risk moves from visitors to our own traces: raw chat transcripts, routine prompts, box paths, gh auth, corrections mail, and Ryno's private messages. Render only from already-public, CI-scanned repo data, never raw logs.
facts: OWASP LLM02:2025 lists PII leakage, sensitive business data, and exposing system preambles or configuration as disclosure risks.
OWASP recommends least privilege, restricting data sources, and pattern-based redaction before output.
inferences: 'Real execution traces' could tempt us to paste raw run transcripts; those can hold paths, prompts, or tokens.
Our existing CI scans cover data/ and site/, so traces must enter as data/ fields to be scanned.
existing_work: check.py secret and personal-data scans on data/ and site/; push protection
opportunity: Traces = links to merged PRs, chat ids, and research ids only; no raw transcripts, prompts, or usage screenshots
alternatives: Publish raw run logs with manual redaction (rejected; error-prone)
risks: A demo challenge quoting a client-like scenario could invent personal details; use fictional, generic orgs
experiment: Run check.py scans over a draft case file built from PR comments and chat
success_metric: Zero scan hits; no field holds raw transcript text

question: Which interaction failures or misleading states should be tested on the showcase?
finding: Top misleading states: 'live' or 'working now' when the last run was hours ago, demo content read as real work, missing data rendered as zero, stale research shown as current, and broken trace links.
facts: NN/g heuristic 1: keep users informed about what is going on through appropriate feedback within reasonable time.
NN/g: when time changes system state, explain it briefly rather than letting items silently change or vanish.
inferences: Every time-based claim needs an 'as of' timestamp from runs.json.
research.json fresh_until gives a free stale check.
existing_work: Post-deploy check after every merge; empty states (#25)
opportunity: Test fixtures: stale runs.json, an expired fresh_until, a demo item, a missing count; each must render honestly
alternatives: Manual spot checks after deploy only
risks: Fixtures can drift from real data; build them from copies of real files
experiment: Render the home page with a runs.json whose last run is 3 days old and check the wording
success_metric: No page says live/now/today unless runs.json supports it; demos always carry a Demo label

question: Which outcomes would show the showcase is working, without visitor tracking and using only existing data?
finding: We can't measure impressed visitors without tracking, so measure proof quality instead: share of showcase claims with a linked artifact, Trial-verified acceptance rate, research-to-ship rate, and caught-before-publish counts.
facts: GitHub repo traffic (views, referrers, popular content) is visible only to people with push access and covers the past 14 days.
That traffic graph covers the repository, not the Pages site.
inferences: Repo traffic is the only existing visitor signal and it is owner-only and partial; it should not drive design.
Existing data already gives: all 10 shipped team ideas (i10-i15, i17-i20) have Trial acceptance checks; Verify dropped 10 of 30 backfill candidates.
existing_work: Analyst research metrics in the tracker: research-to-approval, approval-to-ship, experiment success
opportunity: A proof-coverage check in build: count claims with and without artifact links per page
risks: Proxy metrics can be gamed by adding links; Lens spot-checks that links support the claim
experiment: Count linked vs unlinked claims on the current home page by hand
success_metric: 100% of showcase claims link an artifact; reported weekly by Analyst

question: What do interactive demos cost to run and keep reliable inside free-tier and pacing limits?
finding: Hosting is not the constraint: static pages cost nothing extra on Pages and public-repo CI. Slopbot usage is: each demo challenge is a research session. Cap it at one demo challenge per sprint, 4-5 roles, about 15 reads.
facts: GitHub Pages: 1 GB site, soft 100 GB/month bandwidth, soft 10 builds/hour.
GitHub Actions on standard hosted runners: 6-hour job limit and 20 concurrent jobs on Free; our CI finishes in under 2 minutes.
inferences: This round used 15 page reads for 14 roles, our first real per-round cost figure.
Pre-rendered demos have no runtime failure modes beyond broken links, which the link check covers.
existing_work: Run budget in runs.json; research is the first optional work cut
opportunity: Budget line for demo challenges on the schedule page; Sweep logs reads per challenge
alternatives: Re-run demos on a schedule (wasteful; they are point-in-time)
risks: Usage is Ryno's plan allowance; a big challenge could crowd out the daily run
experiment: Log reads and session time for the first demo challenge and compare with this round
success_metric: Each demo challenge stays under about 15 reads and never delays the 9:13 daily run

question: Which lessons from real failures, ours and public ones, should shape the showcase design?
finding: Public lesson: a company is liable for what its AI says, static page or chatbot alike. Ours: guardrails held when filters hit the input ban, a duplicate PR (#21/#22), X rate limits. We have never reverted a deploy, so don't stage one.
facts: BBC on the Air Canada ruling: the tribunal said it makes no difference whether information comes from a static page or a chatbot; the airline paid damages.
Team history: radio filters hit check.py's input ban and were rebuilt with anchors (c62); #21 was superseded by #22; X search was rate limited on 2026-10-16.
inferences: Demo challenge outcomes must read as worked examples, not advice or quotes.
Showing our real, small failures is more credible than a staged dramatic one.
existing_work: Friday retro rules; runs.json logs drops, strips, and CI failures
opportunity: A 'what went wrong and how we caught it' strip using only real incidents, plus a demo disclaimer on every challenge
alternatives: A dramatized failure demo (rejected; it never happened)
risks: A short failure list may read as 'nothing ever goes wrong'; say plainly that the history is young
experiment: List every real failure in git and runs.json and check each has a link
success_metric: Every failure shown links its commit, PR, or run; zero staged incidents

question: Which of this round's findings duplicate, conflict with, or repeat prior work?
finding: Consolidated 13 reports into 5 concepts. Merged: Forge's Arena + Verify's labels; Scoutmaster's explorer + Critic's real-cases challenge (case files); Trial + Advisor on honest status. Prior work: home intro (#23), facts/inferences split (#20).
facts: ADR practice: record each decision with its rationale, trade-offs, and consequences, kept together as a decision log.
Duplicate pairs found: Arena/labels, explorer/case files, status honesty (Trial/Advisor), cost cap (Sweep/Atlas).
inferences: No finding conflicts with a prior decision; Critic's 'cases before demos' reorders but doesn't reject the CEO's demo challenges.
Behind the scenes already serves as the deep technical ops layer; reuse it, don't rebuild.

question: Which concept best balances differentiation, feasibility, and client value?
finding: Research Arena first (priority 40), then real case files (12.5), then the outcome-led landing and Living Team (10), then one demo challenge after a cost experiment (3.3). Impact Ledger and Build Observatory wait for real data.
facts: Intercom's RICE adds a confidence factor to curb enthusiasm for exciting but ill-defined ideas.
RICE notes dependencies can justify working out of score order, as long as the trade-off is explicit.
inferences: Our Evidence score plays RICE's confidence role; demo challenges score low on it until one is run.
The landing depends on Arena and case files existing, so it ships third despite high impact.
existing_work: Librarian's consolidated set; Critic's challenge; i10 home intro
alternatives: All five experiences at once; landing first
risks: Sprint exceeds the 1 feature + 1 design PR/week cap without a CEO override
experiment: Run demo challenge 1 inside the research cap before building its page
success_metric: Showcase answers the 3 CEO questions with every claim linked to a real artifact
